newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-AT&T a Cinderella as market has a ball.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-AT&T a Cinderella as market has a ball.

text.p: AT&T Corp shares, considered unattractive by most analysts, were left behind on Tuesday while the broad market swept to the second highest gain ever.

The nation's biggest long distance company closed 1-1/8 or 3.4 percent lower at $32, depressed by even weaker than expected first quarter results on Monday. Adjusted for 1996 spin-offs this is a level AT&T stock has not seen since 1993.
"Its hard to find the silver lining in AT&T," said Richard Klugman of Goldman Sachs.
While AT&T stock was avoided by most investors, the Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 173 points on Tuesday to an unofficial close of 6833, its second largest points gain ever.
AT&T on Monday said net profits for the first quarter from continuing operations fell 25 percent, and warned that they would slip a little further in the second quarter.
While long distance showed the expected depradations from falling rates and fierce competition, traditionally robust areas like wireless failed to grow as fast as the marketplace.
"People are starting to realize that AT&T has not got complete control of its destiny," said Klugman.

Analysts say AT&T cannot yet show when the billions it is pouring into entering new markets will bear fruit, and when the results from its core long distance and wireless operations will bounce back against ever stronger rivals.
"AT&T is having trouble in the core business and it will be at least a quarter before we can see where the turnaround point will be," said Guy Woodlief of Prudential Research.
Companies like GTE Corp and fast-growing resellers like Excel Communications Inc have already taken a bite out of AT&T's customer base, both by gaining customers and easing rates lower.
But AT&T has yet to face its toughest rivals, a legion of deep-pocketed regional Bells whose brand names are already familiar to their local customers.

The Bells are expected to gradually gain access to the long distance market in the second half of the year under the terms of the 1996 Telecommunications Act as their reward for opening their own local markets to competition.

AT&T, MCI Communications Corp and Sprint Corp are gradually offering local calling services to customers, but progress has been hindered they say by backlogs in regional Bells handling of customers who want to switch.
If AT&T stock continues to fall the cushion will eventually come from the dividend, which is a four percent yield based on Tuesday's price, analysts say.
"It (the stock) has to be getting close to the bottom now," said Woodlief. However he expected that many shareholders will wait before taking the plunge.
"As they say on the street 'Never try to catch a falling knife'," Woodlief said. ((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))
